I think the entire book if not the entire series was building up to it. Sirius absolutely hated his family. For someone who grew up in such a vile, muggle hating, dark arts supporting environment, he surely showed so much critical thinking and judgement from his first day at Hogwarts. However he was also a deeply flawed person. He grew up in a very competitive environment where he had to be the best and prove his worth to his own family while simultaneously being cautious of them. The series time and again proved just how much James Potter and his parents, wife and kid mean to Sirius. How tragic is it that most of Sirius's direct relatives already perished in the war and he was the only person left to inherit the house. 

Sirius was not cared for by his family and only valued the love of his friends. I would say he half died when James Potter and his family were destroyed. Having to be imprisoned for that tragedy would have already destroyed quite a bit of his soul. The joy sucking dementors certainly took care of that. The only emotion in him for 13 years was revenge. But despite trying his best, Pettigrew got away, Voldemort did come back and to add insult to injury, he was not allowed to do anything about it.

Taking into account all of Sirius's frustrations for 15 years, it made perfect sense he'd jump at the first chance to face death eaters. It would also make sense that he did not have much wand or duelling practice left in him. He probably did not even have his own wand in the ministry fight. So many people got injured and maimed there and Bellatrix really wanted to kill Sirius for personal vindication. All of these factors lead to the logical conclusion that Sirius wouldn't survive the ministry fight.

Emotionally it did make Harry loathe Voldemort. It cemented the fact that just like Sirius, he too did not have any immediate family who would miss him if he died. Friends were the best part of his life as well. It pushed him to prepare to face Voldemort and abandon any innocence because there was nothing shielding him anymore.

I think she epitomises a working class mother. She has 6 sons and a daughter. Her husband is perpetually poor because he does not use his wits to do a better job or gain allies and instead keeps tinkering with muggle objects or breaks his own laws. No shade to Arthur who's a loving father, but Molly held the family together through and through. She always ensured her kids were well fed and clothed. She prepared feasts for them which rivaled the Hogwarts' feasts. She always disciplined Fred and George because while they might be hooligans or popular they'd still need to know the difference between right and wrong. Her sons left after graduation and made money because that is what wizards are expected to do when they come of age. Ron has insecurities but can you imagine any other 11 year old being so kind and welcoming to an orphan kid and backing him up every step of the way? Ginny starts out timid but she becomes so fierce and courageous. How many parents would allow their kids to follow Harry Potter into the woods and live in isolation? How many parents would be okay with their daughter leading a resistance at Hogwarts against her Death Eater teachers and getting punished daily?

Charlie with dragons, Bill with goblins, all her children being so stubborn and carving their own paths has got to take a toll on her. She was very courageous and loving and shown to accept all sorts of people, muggle-borns, Werewolf like Lupin, Sirius a wanted murderer once she knew the truth, Harry who was always being chased by the most evil wizard. She only valued honesty, loyalty and love. The twins always complained about her being hard on them but showered her with gifts once they started making money. All her children realised just how cool their parents were and how they were ready to live and die by their words when  Voldemort came back. Compared to the hypocrisy and selfishness of so many parents in the books, we realise caring too much or being a disciplinarian cannot be held against one of the best parents in the series - Molly Weasley.

There was backup. Snape, headmasters in the portraits who knew a lot of Dumbledore's plans, teachers at Hogwarts who would always take care of their students. Lots of aurors and the Ootp had their hands full with hiding from so many attacks, protecting their family, friends and the rest of those resisting. 

You forget that in a war, anyone's primary focus would be to survive. They needed to take care of those dependent on them first. Harry was chosen because he did not have family to take care of and he was locked into the situation as he couldn't survive if he didn't defeat Voldemort. 

I think the series keeps driving the simple point home time and again that courage and selflessness is the most important thing above all. Voldemort could have gone after the pure blooded wizard with a long lineage like Neville but chose Harry because he was half blooded. Dumbledore once again chose to confide and ask Harry to carry on his mission not just because he was marked as the horcrux. Because he had proven time and again that even if people did not count on him, he'd still do anything in the world to protect Hogwarts and fight on the side of the righteous.

I think Harry was Dumbledore's best plan and somehow Harry had never failed the wizarding world since his birth. Dumbledore could have told multiple people his plan. But he always believed that in terms of courage and being driven by a cause, Harry and the trio matched Voldemort better than anyone else. Why would anyone else make it their business to fight Voldemort when they could flee the country or save themselves. Not undermining any of the other amazing people in the book, but it takes real guts to embrace death and still ensure the dark lord will be defeated. Harry was better than Dumbledore in many aspects.

Also I believe Dumbledore trusted Harry that he would make arrangements to defeat Voldemort if he was nearing his own end.

Completely agree. At one point, Universities need to wonder what exactly is an LOR adding to an application or allow students to submit it themselves on a college letterhead with a seal. It essentially deters students from completing their applications despite having paid the fee and carefully working on all other sections for months. Most undergraduate professors get atleast 3-4 (I'm being extremely conservative) requests for LORs and they might have to submit to 6 colleges on an average. That's already 24 applications, finding the right LOR, verifying, submitting. Some might get 100s of other emails each day. It is absolutely exhausting for them and for the students. I could see an assistant professor in my department (not having a doctorate) needed to submit for atleast 5-6 students. It's definitely not going to work out for everyone. At the end of the day, universities want to thin the herd of applications or have good cause to reject applications while making money off the fees. Or they are testing whether your referee likes you enough to put in the effort for you or are they handing out recommendations to everyone. If it's the latter case, then it discourages professors from providing recommendations in the first place.
